以连绵开张的一笔书拓展父法，与王羲之并称二王。: With a continuous and continuous stroke of calligraphy, he expanded on his father's style, and together with Wang Xizhi, was known as one of the Two Wangs.
《瘗鹤铭》宽博疏宕、篆意入楷，历来归属有争议，清代碑学尤重其气象。: The 'Inscription on the Crane Buried' is broad, sparse, and free-flowing, with seal script meaning integrated into regular script. Its attribution has long been debated, and Qing dynasty stele studies especially valued its grandeur.

以奔涌连绵的狂草开拓抒情书写，与怀素并称颠张醉素。: He pioneered and lyrical writing with surging, wild cursive script, and together with Huai Su, was known as 'Dianzhang, Zui Su.'

以厚实笔力与纵逸狂草打破拘谨，是吴门书派最具奔放气质的代表之一。: With his robust brushwork and free-spirited cursive to break restraint, he is one of the most unrestrained representatives of the Wu School of calligraphy.
以连绵轴线、强烈欹侧和浓淡涨墨重塑长篇行草，是明清之际的重要革新者。: Reconstructing long running and cursive scripts with continuous axes, strong leaning, and varying ink tones, he was an important innovator at the Ming and Qing transitions.
以隶法入篆、以碑意融帖，拓展清代篆隶书写的表现力。: By incorporating clerical script into seal script and blending the meaning of steles with model script, he expanded the expressive power of Qing dynasty seal and clerical script writing.
以碑骨融入行草，并整理推广标准草书，让草法走向易识易写。: Integrating stele bone into running and cursive script, and organizing and promoting standard cursive script, making cursive style easier to recognize and write.
以长线牵引、开张错落的行草书写诗词，形成鲜明的个人书写面貌。: He writes poetry with long, varied running and cursive scripts with long lines and open strokes, forming a distinctive personal style.

The silk manuscript of Laozi, Volume A, is a complete ancient manuscript from the early Han dynasty and serves as the most core first-hand material for collating and extending the Laozi, filling the textual evolution gap between the Warring States Guodian Chu slips and the Wei-Jin Wang Bi circulation edition; Comparing with the earlier Guodian Chu bamboo slips, one can also observe the evolution of the Dao De Jing's thought and writing over more than a hundred years from the Warring States period to the early Han dynasty, providing key evidence for clarifying the early relationship between Confucianism and Daoism.

1. Reversed order of the two parts (maximum structural difference)
Silk manuscript Edition A: The Classic of Virtue comes first, the Classic of Dao follows. The opening line is Chapter 38 of the Universal Edition: 'The highest virtue is not virtuous, and thus there is virtue.' You have to read up to 93 lines to reach the first chapter of the standard edition, "The Way Can Be Taken."
The Tongxing Wang Bi edition: The Dao Classic comes first, the Virtue Classic follows. The opening says, "The Dao can be speak, but the eternal Dao" is present, first discussing the origin of the universe, then on virtue, governing the country, and cultivating oneself.

2. Avoid taboo taboos and change characters; replace keywords: 恒 → 常
In the original text of version A, it is written as Constant Way, Constant Without Desire, Constant Desire; Emperor Wen of Han's given name was Liu Heng. Later generations copied and changed 'Heng' to 'Chang' to avoid naming taboos.
Version A: Not the eternal path | Common version: The eternal path.
This is not a copying error, but a mandatory ancient taboo system, which brings subtle differences in the meaning of words.

3. A large number of sentence-ending function words "也" were preserved; the standard edition mostly deleted it, making the style more concise
The sentence structure of Section A naturally contains the classical Chinese relaxed mood particle: 'Dao' means to be spoken of, not to be eternal. A name can be named, but it is not a permanent name.
The Tongxing edition removes all "也": the Dao can be said, but the eternal Dao; A name that can be named is not an eternal name.
The function word itself does not change its core meaning, but its rhythm and nuance differ; The Jia version is closer to the pre-Qin colloquial style of written expression, while the common version is the later condensed and polished text.

4. Textual changes in Chapter 19 are key to understanding the evolution of Confucian-Daoist relations (Guodian slips can serve as corroborating)
The silk inscription is the first edition: sever sages and abandon wisdom, the people's benefits multiply a hundredfold; Abandoning benevolence and righteousness, the people return to filial piety and kindness, consistent with the standard text.
An even earlier Guodian Chu bamboo slip says: 'Cutting off cleverness and abandoning argument, the people benefit a hundredfold;' Falsehood is completely eliminated and deceit abandoned; the people once again show filial piety and kindness.
It can be seen that the mid-Warring States version did not directly deny "benevolence and righteousness," and there was no sharp opposition between Confucianism and Daoism; It was not until the late Warring States period to the early Han dynasty that the Mawangdui silk edition was revised to "abandon benevolence and righteousness," taking on the intensifying Confucian-Daoist debate. Many later generations used this popular version to amplify the opposition between Laozi and Confucianism.

5. Rewriting Core Philosophical Sentences: Shifts in Cosmology and Political Views (Circumvented by the Guodian Slips)
(1) The sentence 'All things are born': Guo Dian bamboo slip says, 'All things under heaven are born from being, born from non-being'—existence and non-existence coexist, jointly transforming and giving rise to all things; The first edition of the silk manuscript adds a progressive layer, stating 'All things under heaven are born from being, and being is born from non-being,' establishing 'non-being' as the ultimate source of a progressive cosmic framework.
(2) The phrase 'great vessel': the Guo shop slip 'great vessel is fully formed' and the silk manuscript Jia manuscript 'great vessel is exempt from completion' originally means that great vessel is not deliberately artificial or ostentatious; Later generations commonly used this work as a 'late bloomer,' turning it into an inspirational saying emphasizing the accumulation of time.
(3) Regarding governance: Guodian slip "Heaven has many taboos, and the people rebel even more," emphasizing that strict prohibitions would provoke popular resistance; The first edition of the silk manuscript was changed to 'The world is full of taboos, and the people grow poorer,' shifting the focus from 'resistance' to the hardships of the people, with a gentler tone that fits the early Han dynasty's mindset of recuperation and recuperation.

There are discrepancies in the order of sections and sentence wording, and the use of loan characters is extensive
(1) Chapter order: A few chapters have different order, for example, in the standard edition of Chapter 24, in the first edition of the silk manuscript, it is placed before chapter 22;
(2) Example phrases: Version A "Nameless, the beginning of all things"; The standard edition changed it to 'Nameless, the beginning of heaven and earth'; Original A represents "all things," while the common edition is replaced by a higher-level "Heaven and Earth";
(3) Numerous loan characters: Version A heavily uses loan characters (刑 = adjective, 隋 = follows), and the commonly used version uniformly switches to later commonly used characters.

7. There is no fixed eighty-one chapter division
The first edition of the silk manuscript only has a few small dots to separate sentences and paragraphs, lacking the standardized system of eighty-one chapters; The eighty-one chapters were standardized and divided by later editors (between Han and Wei). Wang Bi's edition continued this set of eighty-one chapters, becoming the standard for over a thousand years. Chapter division directly influences later generations' understanding of sentence organization and the division of meanings.
Additional note: The Guodian Chu slips themselves are excerpts, not the complete version of the Laozi, and also include the unique 'Tai Yi Shengshui' (Taiyi Yisheng Shui). This set of Chu cosmological theories is not found in the Mawangdui silk manuscripts, which also indirectly shows that the Laozi texts of the Warring States period were in a state of circulation and multiple branches, not a fixed fixed edition throughout history.
